title: Multiple Timestamp Directories Exist in the Mount Directory After the Server Is Powered Off
body:
### What happened?

Background: I have a K8S cluster, version is v1.25.3, on the master node core1 there is a deployment mounted secret (named ssl). In normal cases, the mount directory in the container is as follows:
![正常挂载](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/66065665/d4f7c38a-e1ac-40bb-b67a-3df5a119498e)
![挂载目录](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/66065665/181387d8-f08f-4782-929e-fa26ff3a6685)
But when I reboot the machine and go to the container to view the mount directory, it looks like this:
![reboot后](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/66065665/4d885d9b-fba6-4892-a090-aa55f2d506ad)
A timestamp directory is generated upon each reboot. The permission of the files in the directory that is not linked by the soft link..data can be changed. In the preceding figure, the permission is changed to 700.
![多次reboot](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/66065665/1cbd218e-192e-4b4c-b8bd-4679f450bf28)
When I restarted the pod, the mount directory was back to normal.
![重弹](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/66065665/73e539c1-c9cd-486c-92c3-1407c527d8af)
While restarting the pod will make this go away, I want to keep only one mounted timestamp directory. If the timestamp directory is not linked by ..data, the permission can be changed. For example, in the preceding figure, the permission is changed to 700 because of this container’s command. If sensitive files exist in the timestamp directory and the permission is too high, the files are insecure for enterprises. In addition, power-off is inevitable.
![配置](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/66065665/81507e7a-5077-40f3-b79f-02dd62c6f68b)
Therefore, I think that there should be only one timestamp directory in the power-off scenario. There should not be a timestamp directory whose permissions can be changed and that contains sensitive files when mounting secrets.


### What did you expect to happen?

Only One Timestamp Directory Exists in the Mount Directory After the Linux Machine Is Powered Off

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Mount the projection data volume to the container and reboot the linux machine.

### Anything else we need to know?

I added the log in atomic_write.go and then I rebooted the linux machine. By looking at the kubelet logs, I know that the reason the old timestamp directory wasn't deleted was because it didn't successfully get the directory pointed to by ..data.

I add the log in the code like this：
![代码](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/66065665/a94a8541-400d-4ca1-8032-6db6a58bc683)
After the machine is rebooted, there is a log like this:
```
-------dataDirPath is /var/lib/kubelet/pods/01352a44-7d9e-445d-940f-7653118abc8c/volumes/kubernetes.iowsecret/ssl/..data ------
-------oldTsDir is  -------
-------oldTsPath is /var/lib/kubelet/pods/01352a44-7d9e-445d-940f-7653118abc8c/volumes/kubernetes.iowsecret/ssl -------
```
After the code  `oldTsDir, err := os.Readlink(dataDirPath)`  is executed, the value of variable `oldTsDir` is empty.


### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"25+", GitVersion:"v1.25.3", GitCommit:"cadee57c0b4d8d8ba9eb45e30d29eba749a87452", GitTreeState:"dirty", BuildDate:"2023", GoVersion:"go1.20.7", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Kustomize Version: v4.5.7
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"25+", GitVersion:"v1.25.3", GitCommit:"cadee57c0b4d8d8ba9eb45e30d29eba749a87452", GitTreeState:"dirty", BuildDate:"2023", GoVersion:"go1.20.7", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

```

title: runtime.ToUnstructured: panics for nil slice in map
body:
### What happened?

I'm implementing a new API (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123516). Part of that API is a one-of-many struct which contains as one option a slice. Empty or nil slice are different from "field not set", so I need to use a pointer. Because gogo/protobuf has a problem handling `*[]string`, I'm using a wrapper struct.

With those types, encoding as unstructured fails:
```

reflect.flag.mustBeAssignable(...)

...
```

/sig api-machinery

### What did you expect to happen?

No panic, round-trip works.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this patch:

title: [Bug] framework.Event not working when Node was added
body:
### What happened?

T1: My pod failed scheduling because of InterPodAffinity:
```
I0226 17:55:16.511750       1 schedule_one.go:188] "Status after running PostFilter plugins for pod" pod="default/nginx-anti-affinity-766965866-fpxqx" status="preemption: 0/2 nodes are available: 1 No victims found on node cn-shenzhen.10.0.3.86 for preemptor pod nginx-anti-affinity-766965866-fpxqx, 1 No victims found on node cn-shenzhen.10.0.5.157 for preemptor pod nginx-anti-affinity-766965866-fpxqx., "
```

T2: One node was added to cluster by ClusterAutoscaler, and there is a taint {"key":"node.kubernetes.io/not-ready","effect":"NoSchedule"} on node so the pod didn't pass the func preCheckForNode(nodeInfo). This is reasonable:
```
I0226 17:55:31.361891       1 eventhandlers.go:76] "Add event for node" node="cn-shenzhen.10.0.4.9"
```

T3: KCM removed the taints from node, I found the pod was not scheduled:
```
I0226 17:55:50.341010       1 scheduling_queue.go:1104] "Event is not making pod schedulable" pod="default/nginx-anti-affinity-766965866-fpxqx" event="NodeTaintChange"
```
This is the log in my audit:
```
objectRef: {"resource":"nodes","name":"cn-shenzhen.10.0.4.9","apiVersion":"v1"}
requestObject: {"metadata":{"resourceVersion":"33524979"},"spec":{"taints":null}}
requestReceivedTimestamp: 2024-02-26T09:55:50.331949Z
```

Then I found the reason:
We only record the first failed plugin in Filter, so we will miss some event. For example, my pod failed in InterPodAffinity, so TaintToleration was not be executed. InterPodAffinity only return Queue for `{Event: framework.ClusterEvent{Resource: framework.Node, ActionType: framework.Add | framework.UpdateNodeLabel}}`, so my pod did not be scheduled until it was refreshed from unschedulable queue after 5 minutes.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod which failed scheduling due to InterPodAffinity should be rescheduled when a new node was added to cluster.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Just see what happend section.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
# paste output here
```
1.28.3
And I think there is the same problem because the code is not changed.

/cc @liggitt
/sig node

Quota (like all kube API constructs) is eventually consistent.  The race noted here where 

1. there are 14 pods, quota is set to max 15, quota has a current count of 14
2. pod is created and admission increments a count to 15
3. the resource quota controller reconciles before observing the pod create and sets the observed value to 14
4. another pod is created and admission increments a count to 15

can happen in such a system.  Eventually the count will be reconciled to 16 (I think `--resource-quota-sync-period` is 5m by default).

While with enough live interlocks this could be avoided, it would be too costly to use on a live server.  The current behavior is within design parameters.  The race is impractical to exploit in a useful way because it is difficult to predict the exact timing of the resync and changes are disruptive. If you have a design that would keep the performance profile of quota consistent and close the race, please bring it to the apimachinery meeting (agenda [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1x9RNaaysyO0gXHIr1y50QFbiL1x8OWnk2v3XnrdkT5Y/edit)).  

/close

title: The pod remains in the terminating state for an extended period of time
body:
### What happened?

When Kubernetes starts a pod, if the pod is deleted while it is still pulling the image, the pod will remain in the terminating state until the image pull is completed before it gets deleted. If the image is large, the waiting time can be particularly long.

### What did you expect to happen?

When deleting a pod, delete it directly without waiting for the image download to complete.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Prepare a relatively large image and ensure it has not been loaded on the Kubernetes node. Start a pod with this image, and delete the pod while it is in the process of pulling the image.

title: HPA External metrics with `metricType: AverageValue` don't correctly count the number of pods
body:
### What happened?

When using an HPA with an external metric with `metricType: AverageValue`, it calculated the ratio of desired-to-actual by looking at the scale sub-resource's `.status.replicas`.
This caused an issue during a rolling deploy with `Deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge: 50%` and `Deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable: 0%` since the scale sub-resources `.status.replicas` will be inflated by up to 1.5x, which incorrectly tells the HPA to scale the workload down.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the number of pods used when calculating the ratio of desired-to-actual to match the algorithm described in https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/#algorithm-details.
Generally, I would expect only Ready pods to be counted, similar to the behaviour for Pod metrics.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I'm unable to get it to reproduce consistently, but the main issue is the code itself which I'll link the code flow below. I'll give a brief overview on how I reproduced it, but it's flaky and you can honestly skip this and understand the issue better by looking at the code I outline in `Anything else we need to know?`.

<details>

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: mydeployment
  namespace: foobar
  labels:
    app: ubuntu
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ubuntu
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ubuntu
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: ubuntu
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command:
                - sh
                - -c
                - test -f /tmp/ready.txt
            initialDelaySeconds: 65
          command:
            - /bin/bash
            - -c
            - --
          args:
            - while true; do sleep 30; touch /tmp/ready.txt; done
          image: ubuntu:jammy
          imagePullPolicy: Always
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0%
      maxSurge: 50%
```

Then you need an HPA with a static metric and short scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds, you can achieve this using Keda. To be clear, this is not specific to Keda, it's just a way to get a metric that always returns a value of `25`. This ScaledObject will create an external metric for the fallback with a `metricType: AverageValue`.

```yaml
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: myscaledobject
  namespace: foobar
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    kind: Deployment
    name: mydeployment
  advanced:
    horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig:
      behavior:
        scaleDown:
          stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
          policies:
            - type: Pods
              value: 10
              periodSeconds: 15
  fallback:
    failureThreshold: 1
    replicas: 25
  pollingInterval: 15
  minReplicaCount: 10
  maxReplicaCount: 50
  triggers:
  - type: prometheus
    name: invalid_trigger
    metricType: AverageValue
    metadata:
      serverAddress: http://fake.svc.cluster.local:9090
      threshold: "1"
      activationThreshold: "0"
      query: >
        max(mymetric1{}[2m])
```

After doing many deployments, eventually you'll see it scale down. You can also do a `kubectl get hpa -w` to see the target ratio be something like `0.673m/1.0` during a deploy. 

</details>

### Anything else we need to know?

Here is the code flow for the HPA:

1. [computeReplicasForMetric](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/015e76aa24ebfebfd64062e1161059ac62ddabc9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L424) is called
2. Which takes [this branch](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/015e76aa24ebfebfd64062e1161059ac62ddabc9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L488-L489)
3. [computeStatusForExternalMetric](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/015e76aa24ebfebfd64062e1161059ac62ddabc9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L685) is called
4. Which takes [this branch](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/015e76aa24ebfebfd64062e1161059ac62ddabc9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L686-L687)
5. [GetExternalPerPodMetricReplicas](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/015e76aa24ebfebfd64062e1161059ac62ddabc9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L354) is called
6. Which calculates a replica count [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/015e76aa24ebfebfd64062e1161059ac62ddabc9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L368-L375)
7. [Which uses the raw statusReplicas](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/015e76aa24ebfebfd64062e1161059ac62ddabc9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L368) value when calculating the desired-to-actual ratio
8. statusReplicas can be traced back to [scale.Status.replicas](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/015e76aa24ebfebfd64062e1161059ac62ddabc9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L307) which gets the status replicas on the scale sub-resource of the deployment. This includes unready pods.

However, the [Kubernetes documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/#algorithm-details) says the algorithm for `metricType: AverageValue` should list the pods in the scale target, then filter out unready pods and terminating pods (I'm simplifying for brevity), and use that value as the available replicas when calculating the ratio.

title: Unable to Create Headless Services  in 1.27.3
body:
### What happened?

Getting errors when trying to set `ClusterIP` to `None` in 1.27.3. Likely due to 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115075/files

```
spec:
 ```

title: [kubeadm] Apparently, it's not possible to change the Node CIDR Mask Size
body:
### What happened?

BACKGROUND
I'm trying to create a small HA kubernetes cluster with 'kubeadm" following the topology "stacked control plane nodes" described here [1]. Considering I want to have 3 worker nodes, my infra looks as the following:
 - 6 nodes in total ( 3 control plane and 3 worker ).
 - All 6 nodes are within a GCP /28 subnet. In GCP, the first 2 and last 2 IPs of a subnet are unusable for the user. Meaning my cluster can run up to 12 nodes (16 - 2 - 2).
 - I'm also running an internal TCP Load Balancer with an internal IP within the same /28 subnet to distribute the traffic within the 3 control plane nodes, that leaves a total space of 11 nodes for the cluster.
 - Moving on, I decided to have a maximum number of pods per node of 64. For that, I have created a /20 secondary IPv4 range in the subnet, that I can divide into up to 16 /26 alias IP ranges for each node of my cluster.
 - I follow the same strategy for the services CIDR, I want a max of 64 per node, therefore I create a /20 secondary IPv4 range that I can later divide 16 times for each node as /26 alias Ip ranges.

ISSUE
When installing the cluster on the 1st control plane node, when I get to the step of running the command:
 $ sudo kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint "192.168.0.7:6443" --upload-certs --pod-network-cidr "172.16.0.0/26" --service-cidr "172.16.4.0/26"
I get the error:
 networking.podSubnet: Invalid value: "172.16.0.0/26": the size of pod subnet with mask 26 is smaller than the size of node subnet with mask 24

The thing is, the node subnet mask is not 24, but 28 ( see 2 bulletpoint in background ). I've tried several ways to change this value without success:
 - Via a now deprecated `kubeadm init` flag: --node-cidr-mask-size 28
 - Via providing a kubeadm configuration file [2] via the flag: --config
___
[1]
https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kubeadm/ha-topology/#stacked-etcd-topology
[2]
https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/kubeadm-config.v1beta3/

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect to be able to configure the Node CIDR Mask Size ( value other than 24 ) during the `kubeadm init` command step. Apparently, this was possible in the past with the flag `--node-cidr-mask-size`, see [3].
___
[3]
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/111425#issuecomment-1195076050

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Trying to mimic a topology like the one described in background:
 - Up to 16 nodes in the cluster ( /28 ).
 - Up to 64 pods per node ( subnet secondary range of /20, that gives enough space for 16 /26 alias ip ranges for all possible 16nodes in the cluster ).
 - Same topology for the services CIDR.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Pod looses network connection (connection reset errors) during preStop period
body:
### What happened? **Environment:** I am running an Spring boot HTTP server and an HTTP client pod, where the client sends requests to the server using the `myserver.svc.cluster.local` address. Both server and client communicate over a keep-alive session. And the server is configured with a `preStop` hook set to 10 seconds during rolling updates ``` A(pod)--- | -- myserver(svc) <--[HTTP request with keep-alive]-- myclient(svc) --- C(pod) B(pod)--- ``` **Issue:** When performing a rolling update on the `myserver`, the client experiences a 2 times of a connection reset error. Each connection reset error occurs immediately as the each server pod enter the Terminating state. (beginning of preStop session)
**Detailed condition:** Despite the preStop being set to 10 seconds, which should theoretically allow existing keep-alive sessions to continue without accepting new HTTP traffic, the server's IP is immediately removed from the endpoints upon the preStop hook initiation. As a result, keep-alive sessions, which should have been maintained with Pod A, are transferred to Pod B. **ex)** For example, the client sends an HTTP GET request with a sequence number `61293`, which was associated with a keep-alive session on Pod A. However, as soon as preStop on Pod A initiates, this packet is redirected to Pod B. Pod B, receiving a packet with an unexpected sequence number, sends an RST packet back to the client, resulting in a connection reset error. ### What did you expect to happen? While I expect that new HTTP traffic will not reach the pod during the preStop period, **I also expect that existing keep-alive sessions should be preserved.** However, this is not happening. Is this a bug, or is it intended behavior? ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? . ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version v1.15.11 ```
### Cloud provider
kubernetes inhouse closed cloud service

```console # On Linux: $ cat /etc/os-release # paste output here $ uname -a # paste output here # On Windows: C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture # paste output here ```

title: Difference in observed pod status in regular vs static pod
body:
### What happened?

I was looking create a reproducer to test https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122778, when I stumbled upon something that didn't make sense to me. Maybe I am mistaken, please feel free to close this issue if it isn't a real bug. 

I was trying to force the pod to stay in `ContainerCreating` state for debugging https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122721 when using standard `Generic PLEG`.  So I modified `Generic PLEG` in my local setup to ignore `PodLifeCycle ContainerStarted` event for a specific pod under test using this patch, 

<details>
  <summary>pleg diff</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go b/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go
index 80da5bb059c..3ec180ec0a6 100644
--- a/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go
+++ b/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go
@@ -19,6 +19,7 @@ package pleg
 import (
        "context"
        "fmt"
+       "strings"
        "sync"
        "sync/atomic"
        "time"
@@ -176,7 +177,7 @@ func (g *GenericPLEG) Healthy() (bool, error) {
        return true, nil
 }
 
-func generateEvents(podID types.UID, cid string, oldState, newState plegContainerState) []*PodLifecycleEvent {
+func generateEvents(podID types.UID, cid string, oldState, newState plegContainerState, pod *kubecontainer.Pod) []*PodLifecycleEvent {
        if newState == oldState {
                return nil
        }
@@ -184,6 +185,9 @@ func generateEvents(podID types.UID, cid string, oldState, newState plegContaine
        klog.V(4).InfoS("GenericPLEG", "podUID", podID, "containerID", cid, "oldState", oldState, "newState", newState)
        switch newState {
        case plegContainerRunning:
+               if strings.Contains(pod.Name, "nginx") {
+                       return []*PodLifecycleEvent{{ID: podID, Type: ContainerChanged, Data: cid}}
+               }
                return []*PodLifecycleEvent{{ID: podID, Type: ContainerStarted, Data: cid}}
        case plegContainerExited:
                return []*PodLifecycleEvent{{ID: podID, Type: ContainerDied, Data: cid}}
@@ -388,14 +392,17 @@ func getContainersFromPods(pods ...*kubecontainer.Pod) []*kubecontainer.Containe
 
 func computeEvents(oldPod, newPod *kubecontainer.Pod, cid *kubecontainer.ContainerID) []*PodLifecycleEvent {
        var pid types.UID
+       var pod *kubecontainer.Pod
        if oldPod != nil {
                pid = oldPod.ID
+               pod = oldPod
        } else if newPod != nil {
                pid = newPod.ID
+               pod = newPod
        }
        oldState := getContainerState(oldPod, cid)
        newState := getContainerState(newPod, cid)
-       return generateEvents(pid, cid.ID, oldState, newState)
+       return generateEvents(pid, cid.ID, oldState, newState, pod)
 }

 
 func (g *GenericPLEG) cacheEnabled() bool { 
```
</details>


While this works well for regular pod (which end up getting stuck, as expected, in `ContainerCreating` state), 

```bash
 kubectl get pods 
NAME    READY   STATUS              RESTARTS   AGE
nginx   0/1     ContainerCreating   0          2s
```
but if I deploy the same pod as a static pod it ends up running even though Generic PLEG is clearly not sending any `ContainerStarted` PodLifeCycle event. 

```bash
$ kubectl get pods 
NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-127.0.0.1   1/1     Running   0          2s
```

I always thought the pod status should be similar for regular and static pod, but not sure why do they differ here though. 

<details>
<summary> pod yaml </summary>

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    env: test
```

Please note that this is not really a `bug` per say, that a regular user will encounter. I am deliberately modifying `Generic PLEG` for understanding a few things. Having said that, I was surprised to see a difference in behaviour between regular and static pods under similar modified circumstances.
/cc @smarterclayton
/cc @pacoxu
@tallclair
cc: @SergeyKanzhelev
/triage accepted

I tried reproducing this with the patch but couldn't. Both the regular and the static pods in my cluster ended up in the running state after a while. 

My interpretation is that even though the events weren't sent to trigger an immediate sync for the pod, the pod status are still updated internally in PLEG. And also the fallback sync interval will eventually trigger a full sync of the pod and send the status update to the apiserver. 

Could you try reproducing again and watch the pod status for, say, 5 minutes, to see if you still observe the same problem?

@harche thanks for the update. 

With the information, I think we can all agree that this is not a bug. And even with the change, eventually all pods became running (which is good).

As to why it takes longer for a regular pod in this situation, I have a theory after scanning the log further. 

Logs handling a static pod:
```
kubelet[26439]: I0222 18:20:10.727900   26439 kubelet.go:2408] "SyncLoop ADD" source="file" pods=["default/nginx-gke-otter-default-pool-7dffbbd1-99cz"]
kubelet[26439]: I0222 18:20:10.840722   26439 kubelet.go:2408] "SyncLoop ADD" source="api" pods=["default/nginx-gke-otter-default-pool-7dffbbd1-99cz"]
kubelet[26439]: I0222 18:20:11.774599   26439 kubelet.go:2421] "SyncLoop RECONCILE" source="api" pods=["default/nginx-gke-otter-default-pool-7dffbbd1-99cz"]
kubelet[26439]: I0222 18:21:12.802814   26439 kubelet.go:2459] "SyncLoop (SYNC) pods" total=1 pods=["default/nginx-gke-otter-default-pool-7dffbbd1-99cz"]
```

The first sync happened when kubelet detected the static pod (source=file). At the end of this sync, a mirror pod was created at the apiserver. 
The second sync happened when kubelet detected the mirror pod from the apiserver, this triggered a sync (source=api) right away which resulted in a status update. This is the extra sync that the regular pods don't have. 

I think you should be able to verify the behavior by changing and/or injecting some log messages.

Thanks @yujuhong

somewhat related to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120507

> somewhat related to #120507

The scenarios that trigger panic are similar(the apiserver fails to call webhook), but the log shows that the location of panic is different.

/assign @dims
For context of [`k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/filters`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/filters/OWNERS)
Thank you.
/triage accepted

again, full stack logs:
[kube-apiserver-panic.txt](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/14062163/kube-apiserver-panic.txt)
I'll try to test the mr: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114189

Let me try to explain the panic - both goroutines are trying to write to the `Header` of the `ResponseWriter`

first goroutine: This request has timed out, and consequently the `timeout` filter is trying to send a `StatusGatewayTimeout` response to the caller. This is the client facing goroutine from the timeout filter.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8a1abc25cad87333840cd7d54be2efaf31a3177/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/filters/timeout.go#L248-L261

Note that the call to `WriteHeader` is protected by a mutex, that means that if the other goroutine is using the delegated `Responsewriter` object via the `baseTimeoutWriter` adapter, then this panic should not happen.

second goroutine: let's check the other goroutine, it is also trying to write to the `Header` of the `ResponseWriter` object:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8a1abc25cad87333840cd7d54be2efaf31a3177/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/token/cache/cached_token_authenticator.go#L138-L140

Now `warning.AddWarning` uses an unprotected version of the ResponseWriter object:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8a1abc25cad87333840cd7d54be2efaf31a3177/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/warning.go#L31-L37

The `WithWarningRecorder` filter precedes the `timeout` filter in the execution order, so the `recorder` in  `recorder := &recorder{writer: w}` is not using the thread safe `baseTimeoutWriter` implementation.

This is the order today:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8a1abc25cad87333840cd7d54be2efaf31a3177/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/config.go#L944-L955

one quick resolution is to move the `WithWarningRecorder` after the timeout filter: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115282, but there could be code that precedes that needs to write warning?
Also note that the panic mentioned in 115282 `Header called after Handler finished` is not as severe, it does not cause the apiserver to crash. 

For a more proper solution, i think we would want https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114189

any thoughts? /cc @liggitt @wojtek-t

I tend to remove the timeout filter, the sooner the better, and I think the Apiserver panic is the P0-level bug, directly affecting the availability of the cluster

I have cherry-picked [pr114189](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114189) and tested it in my cluster, and I still need to continue to observe for 1-2 days
I opened a minimal WIP fix for the warning writer in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123034 since the timeout filter removal is a much bigger change to reason through

> I opened a minimal WIP fix for the warning writer in #123034 since the timeout filter removal is a much bigger change to reason through

thanks a lot, I will try to test and cherry-pick the above minimal WIP fix in #123034

sorry, I completely overlooked https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115282, I only saw https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114189 and that looked too big to take safely right now

I prefer https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115282 to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123034
Can we backport the fix to 1.28?

> Can we backport the fix to 1.28?

Why 1.28 specifically? I'm not aware of anything that changed in 1.28 that made this more or less prevalent. If this meets backport criteria, going to all active branches could make sense (1.27+)

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

title: validatingadmissionpolicystatus reports error when using spec.variables
body:
### What happened?

When I load a policy definition like this

```yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: loadbalancer.servicenow.net
spec:
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiVersions: ["v1"]
      apiGroups:   [""]
      resources:   ["services"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
  matchConditions:
  - name: "only-loadbalancer-services"
    expression: object.spec.type == "LoadBalancer"
  paramKind:
    apiVersion: control.servicenow.net/v1beta1
    kind: TenantPermission
  variables:
  - name: loadbalancerid
    expression: "'ccm.snowsk8s.servicenow.net/lb-service-id' in object.metadata.annotations ? object.metadata.annotations['ccm.snowsk8s.servicenow.net/lb-service-id'] : 'none'"
  validations:
    - expression: variables.loadbalancerid in params.permissions.loadbalancerid
      reason: Forbidden
      messageExpression: "'Namespace ' + string(namespaceObject.metadata.name) + ' does not have permissions to loadbalancer ' + string(variables.loadbalancerid)"
  failurePolicy: Fail
```


The object is updated with the following status
```yaml
status:
  observedGeneration: 2
  typeChecking:
    expressionWarnings:
    - fieldRef: spec.validations[0].expression
      warning: |
        /v1, Kind=Service: ERROR: <input>:1:1: undeclared reference to 'variables' (in container '')
         | variables.loadbalancerid in params.permissions.loadbalancerid
         | ^
    - fieldRef: spec.validations[0].messageExpression

         | 'Namespace ' + string(namespaceObject.metadata.name) + ' does not have permissions to loadbalancer ' + string(variables.loadbalancerid)
         | ..............................................................................................................^
```

While this error is reported, the policy does seem to be fully functioning

```
k apply -f testing/someones-loadbalancer.yaml   
Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "testing/someones-loadbalancer.yaml": services "idonthavealoadbalancer" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'loadbalancer.servicenow.net' with binding 'deny-non-owning-loadbalancer' denied request: Namespace workload1 does not have permissions to loadbalancer 123someoneelses123
```

title: kubelet: watch of *v1.Pod ended with: very short watch: k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/config/apiserver.go:67: Unexpected watch close - watch lasted less than a second and no items received
body:
### What happened?

We encountered the following situation:

When the performance of etcd decreases, it causes some nodes in the cluster to show "failed to update lease, error: etcdserver: too many requests". At the same time, the client go module reports "watch of * v1. Pod ended with very short watch: k8s. io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/configure/apiserver. go: 67: Unexpected watch close - watch last less than a second and no items received"

### What did you expect to happen?

The client go module should not display a watch of * v1. Pod ended with: very short watch: k8s. io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/configure/apiserver. go: 67: Unexpected watch close - watch last less than a second and no items received

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Disable etcd port

Hope it can be of some help, this error log comes from systemd and the prime culprit is maybe not k8s, if some mount entry that has a target(mountpoint) whose length exceeded 256 bytes in your system mount table, systemd will raise this error when it try to load mount entry from mountinfo into mount units.
So, when you encounter this  error message, you should try to find which mount entry has exceed 256 bytes mountpoint, and try to unmount it.

title: OpenAPI handler fails on duplicated path
body:
### What happened?

When installing the metrics-server to implement the metrics.k8s.io API and the prometheus-adapter to implement the custom.metrics.k8s.io API, it is possible to make the OpenAPI handler fail to initialize with this error log in apiserver: https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/blob/master/pkg/aggregator/aggregator.go#L343
```
handler.go:159] Error in OpenAPI handler: failed to build merge specs: unable to merge: duplicated path /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/pods
handler.go:159] Error in OpenAPI handler: failed to build merge specs: unable to merge: duplicated path /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/{namespace}/pods
handler.go:159] Error in OpenAPI handler: failed to build merge specs: unable to merge: duplicated path /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/nodes
handler.go:159] Error in OpenAPI handler: failed to build merge specs: unable to merge: duplicated path /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/nodes/{name}
handler.go:159] Error in OpenAPI handler: failed to build merge specs: unable to merge: duplicated path /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/nodes
```
This will result in kubectl discovery calls to /openapi/v2 to fail with a 503:

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I can provide exact installation steps if needed, however, a high-level repro is:
- install metrics-server to serve v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io  
- install prometheus-adapter to serve v1beta1.custom.metrics.k8s.io

5. If the PR is unfinished, see how to mark it: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/pull-requests.md#marking-unfinished-pull-requests
-->

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This is an interesting issue that came up from a bug report. Currently, OpenAPI v2 is downloaded and merged from aggregated apiservices in its entirety, filtering for only `/apis/*` endpoints. As a result, any aggregated apiservice can claim they serve another endpoint and will be included in the resulting openapi. This is not usually a problem with overriding built-ins because we have different priorities. However, between apiservices gv priorities are usually the same, and merge order is not as deterministic. Thus, a malicious apiservice may claim they serve something like `/apis/someothergroup/version` despite their gv registered as `/apis/stable.example.com/v1`. This PR fixes that such that only the OpenAPI for an apiservice's registered GV is merged and published.

There is an orthogonal bug in [kube-openapi's merging](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/blame/master/pkg/aggregator/aggregator.go#L73-L75)  but that will be addressed separately. 

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

body:

Patch the pod to change CPU requests, and it is successful:
```
[root@node-x test]# kubectl patch pod tonyaw-pod2 --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"test","resources":{"limits":{"cpu":"31000m"}, "requests":{"cpu":"30000m"}}}]}}'
pod/tonyaw-pod2 patched

```

node request is over 100%:
```
kubectl describe nodes node-x
Allocated resources:
  (Total limits may be over 100 percent, i.e., overcommitted.)
  Resource           Requests       Limits
  --------           --------       ------
  # tonyaw: requests is over 100%
  cpu                33850m (105%)  36 (112%)
  memory             6384Mi (3%)    8532Mi (5%)
  ephemeral-storage  0 (0%)         0 (0%)
  hugepages-1Gi      0 (0%)         0 (0%)
  hugepages-2Mi      0 (0%)         0 (0%)

```

If I use same CPU request to recreate this pod, it will fail because of lacking of resource:
```
Warning  FailedScheduling  43s   default-scheduler  0/1 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu. preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Patch to change resources shall be failed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod, and patch its CPU request to over the total request of node.

nodes.body: /sig node

I can't reopen this issue.
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/38208715/8450a5c2-9976-4a34-a5bc-635cc4950492)
Can you modify a pod's resources using patch?

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/38208715/898ae9f9-d48d-40d4-af7a-e2bfc31d709e)
You probably need the feature toggle turned on.

> Patch to change resources shall be failed.

We should define what we expect to happen. There are two outcomes I could imagine:
1. reject the patch
2. accept the patch provided that there is a lower-priority Pod where preempting it would satisfy the new request, and then:
   - find another Pod to preempt
   - preempt that other Pod
   - satisfy the vertical scaling change

I'd actually expect outcome 2. For example, if I have a high-priority static Pod, it's useful to be able to give it more resources. I could talk to the control plane to evict another Pod, but:
 - the scheduler will use the spare capacity as soon as it's available — that's kind of its role in life
 - what if the API server is degraded and the vertical scaling is an attempt to fix this?

Even if in-place Pod vertical scaling doesn't support static Pods today, we should consider a future where it might, and make sure the design accounts for it.

If folks agree with my thinking here, the bug might not be that node requests can exceed 100%, it's that the kubelet isn't doing the preemption I'd expect as early as I'd hope it to.

@sftim , if there is no lower-priority pod, I assume one pod with same priority will be preempted randomly. Right?
In my product environment, actually we don't use pod priority feature. It means all the pods have same priority.
If we go to option2, other pod on same node will be preempted unintentionally.

Is it possible to combine both option1 and option2 at same time:
1. First time, go with option1 to reject the patch.
2. Second time, a "--force" option can be set. It means user knows preemption will happen, and go to option2 sounds more reasonable.

> If there is no lower-priority pod, I assume one pod with same priority will be preempted randomly. Right?

Let's say the node has 7 pods at priority 123456 (all the same). Node overhead is 1 CPU, each Pod requests 1 vCPU, there are 8 CPUs. You also have plenty of memory.

Now, someone tries to scale one of those Pods, in-place, to request 4 vCPU. You're positing that another same-priority Pod gets preempted.

The options I'd support are:
1. randomly select a same-priority Pod, preempt that selected other Pod, do the vertical scaling
1. reject the vertical scaling request

I don't have a strong opinion about which of those is better.
My soft opinion is to reject the vertical scaling request. There could be an API mechanism to allow forcing the preemption; if we add that support, I expect it wouldn't turn up until late in the beta phase.

> I don't have a strong opinion about which of those is better. My soft opinion is to reject the vertical scaling request. There could be an API mechanism to allow forcing the preemption; if we add that support, I expect it wouldn't turn up until late in the beta phase.

I vote the following solution as I mentioned in previous message:
1. If user doesn't provide "--force" option, reject the vertical scaling request.
2. If user provides a "--force" option, preempt lower priority pod, or a same priority pod randomly.

/assign @tzneal 
/triage accepted

This may actually be an issue with the client reporting reqeust rather than actual allocated values. @tzneal is going to investigate
probably something to look at for beta https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/1287
What does the pod status look like in this case? Specifically interested in the pod.status.resize field.

This is what "Deferred" and "Infeasible" are for in `Pod.status.resize` is for - the request itself is valid (structurally and syntactically) and was passed on to kubelet.  Kubelet can decide whether to do an eviction or just wait for some other pods to exit or just say no.
This seems like WAI unless status is broken?

@pacoxu This issue is getting observed frequently on `ppc arch`.

Link to failure : https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/ppc64le-kubernetes/logs/periodic-kubernetes-unit-test-ppc64le/1755260242423189504

So I dig into it, and I'm sure this is a bug...

In #122435, we introduced this logic in `findNodesThatPassFilters`, and this doesn't consider about extenders
```
	if !sched.hasScoring(fwk) {
		numNodesToFind = 1
	}
```

Say that we have two nodes(node1, node2), some filter plugins but no score plugins.
With this line, we'll return only one node in `findNodesThatPassFilters`, probably `node1` but also probably `node2`(due to we check nodes parallel).

And if we have one extender which rejects node2, we'll fail in `findNodesThatPassExtenders` 
if `findNodesThatPassFilters` returns `node2`, but before  #122435, we'll return both nodes in `findNodesThatPassFilters`, and node2 will pass `findNodesThatPassExtenders` .

I'm not sure if this is included in `1.29.1`, if so, then this is a regression, I think we should just revert it now.
/cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-approvers 
/kind bug
/kind regression

And as we can't stop checking nodes in `findNodesThatPassFilters`.
I think the only performance we can improve is here in `prioritizeNodes`:
Change `if len(extenders) == 0 && !fwk.HasScorePlugins() ` to something like: ` if len(ScoreExtenders) == 0 && !fwk.HasScorePlugins() `
I doubt this will have a considerable improvement, and I'm not sure if we should implement #122435 again.
The default `numNodesToFind` is 100. If it happens to be the case that the extenders reject these 100 nodes, but there is another node that could have fit, we still reach this situation, wouldn't we?

> The default numNodesToFind is 100. If it happens to be the case that the extenders reject these 100 nodes, but there is another node that could have fit, we still reach this situation, wouldn't we?

Yes, I think so. But I don't think this behavior is related to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122435 . So does this affect #123290 ?

Wait, it is related🤦. However, making `numNodesToFind = 1` will Increase the probability of this scenario occurring. And it will greatly increase the time required for this pod to return to normal.

>And as we can't stop checking nodes in findNodesThatPassFilters.

We could also check for `len(extenders) == 0` here. It's less elegant, but seems practical. 

>However, making numNodesToFind = 1 will Increase the probability of this scenario occurring. And it will greatly increase the time required for this pod to return to normal.

Yes, it makes it more likely to hit this.

> We could also check for len(extenders) == 0 here. It's less elegant, but seems practical.

I think more specifically check that no filters are registered.

> The default numNodesToFind is 100. If it happens to be the case that the extenders reject these 100 nodes, but there is another node that could have fit, we still reach this situation, wouldn't we?

The ultimate fix is to continue to check for another `numNodesToFind` until all nodes are checked if `findNodesThatPassExtenders` filters all nodes. But this is not related to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122435

title: Pod Container.Command doesn't respect ulimit set in `etc/bash/bash.rc`
body:
### What happened?

There's a good chance I'm misunderstanding how the command runs against the container, but from what I understand, this is doing `exec -- bin/bash -c <command>` and so I'd expect the ulimit to apply there as well but it doesn't. 


With the following dockerfile:

<details>
<summary> Dockerfile </summary>

```
FROM ubuntu:22.04

ARG DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

RUN echo "ulimit -S -s 65536" >> etc/bash.bashrc && \

SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
```

</details>


Using the following manifest:

<details>
<summary>testpod.yaml</summary>

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  containers:
  - image: test/latest
    name: test
    command: ["/bin/bash", "-c", "ulimit -s"]
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: '2'
        memory: 2Gi
      requests:
        cpu: 250m
        memory: 250Mi
```

</details>

The pod logs show `8192` which is the default value and not the one set in the dockerfile.


### What did you expect to happen?

According to my [research](https://askubuntu.com/questions/815066/whats-the-difference-between-bashrc-and-etc-bash-bashrc), `RUN echo "ulimit -S -s 65536" >> etc/bash.bashrc && \`  should allow all bash instances to have their ulimit set regardless of which user starts the instance. 


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Build the dockerfile and deploy the pod on a cluster.

_No response_

Would it not have been trivial to test this instead of asking me? I provided both dockerfile and pod manifest. What file path could have possibly been missing, there's no reference to any files. Ulimit (literally User Limit) is a built-in Linux shell utility to enforce soft/hard 
resource limits on users. I can go into detailed use cases of why this would be useful on a pod but I don't think that's productive, and no, resource quotas don't do the same thing.

Once the docker container is running (on k8s or docker-native) the correct ulimit is shown. You can 'kubectl exec --stdin --tty test -- /bin/bash' then run the command  'ulimit -s' to confirm.

Hence, the title Pod 'container.command' does not respect... Was chosen.

Maybe this is the wrong place for the issue I guess 😕

Docker works:

```
$ cat Dockerfile 
FROM ubuntu:22.04

ARG DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

RUN echo "ulimit -S -s 65432" >> etc/bash.bashrc

$ docker build -t thockin/ulimited .
Sending build context to Docker daemon  2.048kB
Step 1/3 : FROM ubuntu:22.04
 ---> 3db8720ecbf5
Step 2/3 : ARG DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
 ---> Using cache
 ---> 9a3516bd1bed
Step 3/3 : RUN echo "ulimit -S -s 65432" >> etc/bash.bashrc
 ---> Running in 67f6889526a3
Removing intermediate container 67f6889526a3
 ---> 312dfb1de9d3
Successfully built 312dfb1de9d3
Successfully tagged thockin/ulimited:latest

$ docker run -ti thockin/ulimited:latest
root@5db6a068a0f3:/# ulimit -s
65432
```

and:

```
$ docker exec -ti 5db6a068a0f3 bash
root@5db6a068a0f3:/# ulimit -s
65432
```

but if you force a manual run of bash, though:

```
$ docker exec -ti 5db6a068a0f3 bash -c "ulimit -s"
8192
```

So what's happening?

Bash manpage says:  "An  interactive shell is one started without non-option arguments (unless -s is specified) and without the -c option..."

and also: "When an interactive shell that is not a login shell is started, bash reads and executes commands from /etc/bash.bashrc..."

In other words, by running with -c, you have inadvertently broken yourself.

title: Scheduler evaluates many nodes even if there are no scoring plugins defined
body:
### What happened?

Even when no scoring plugins are defined, scheduler always attempts to find multiple nodes where the pod can run. This is unnecessary (and therefore inefficient) when we know ahead of time that there will be no difference between how those nodes are scored. 

### What did you expect to happen?

If we're going to pick a random node, we can just as well cut short the search after finding the first match.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure scheduler without any scoring plugins and see that mulitple nodes are evaluated anyway.

The issue itself is pre-existing and it's not clear whether it is something to be fixed (or how). This change is modified to exclude the cases when extenders are used.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Skip looking for extra nodes if no scoring plugins and no extenders are defined. As there's no difference in priority between nodes when we don't score them and there's no risk that some won't pass extender filters, there's no point in searching for multiple fitting nodes.

Fixes #122057

title: ReplicaSet naming is inconsistent
body:
### What happened?

When kubernetes is creating a ReplicaSet automatically through a deployment, the suffix added to the deployment name has an inconsistent length. Although this is not necessarily a bug, this can lead to issues in trying to identify ReplicaSets that were created through deployments using, for instance, RegEx.

[This code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9754e404390a8d4e969e17e339586376b6f6ad8f/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L1201) is responsible for creating a suffix string to add to the deployment name to create the ReplicaSet name. The number created by `podTemplateSpecHasher.Sum32()` is any number from 0 to 4,294,967,295. This means the suffix string after the number goes through `rand.SafeEncodeString` ([link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/rand/rand.go#L121)) will have a length of 0 to 10.

### What did you expect to happen?

ReplicaSet names should always have a suffix of consistent length when created automatically via a deployment.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a number of deployments that will in turn create ReplicaSets. On average, 23% of these ReplicaSets will have suffixes of length 9 or shorter instead of the expected 10.

### Anything else we need to know?

An easy solution would be to simply change the code as follows:
```
return rand.SafeEncodeString(fmt.Sprintf("%0*d", 10, podTemplateSpecHasher.Sum32()))
```
There is no risk to a solution like this as it will only go into effect when new ReplicaSet revisions are created and will only make ReplicaSet names more consistent. Any names that would be generated out of a number like 1,234,567 will instead be generated by 0,001,234,567, i.e. there is the same number of possible suffixes as before.

### Kubernetes version

Doesn't really matter but:
```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.28.0
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp: lookup ...: no such host
```


### Cloud provider

Not sure what this means.

I agree, but there's no reason not to add this small quality of life improvement to help identify resources. In large scale systems, looking through all pods and replicasets for their owners may put a unwanted load on the EKS control plane when using the name directly may be a more reasonable solution.

In the end, the proposed change simply makes this option (using names to identify owners) more reliable and consistent.

Additionally, there is a low chance that there is a very low number of characters in the suffix which should be considered a bug as the resource names should be obviously "computer generated", i.e. obvious that they are dependents of other resources. For example, there is a 10/4294967295 chance of having a suffix with a single character. This happens if the hash generates number 0-9.

Proof:
- Golang documentation for Hash shows it generates a uint32: [link](https://pkg.go.dev/hash)
- Code shows the following: [link](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.21.3:src/builtin/builtin.go;l=34)
```
// uint32 is the set of all unsigned 32-bit integers.
// Range: 0 through 4294967295.
type uint32 uint32
```

It can be improved, but using regular expressions to identify ReplicaSets may not be the good approach. This is because the number of random characters is not guaranteed and could change in the future. For example, in the case of Pods, there was an attempt to increase the length of random characters from 5 to 10. In the end, there were several projects relying on parsing random strings, and the PR is currently on hold due to a lack of a good alternative (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116430, https://github.com/gocrane/crane/issues/716).

cc: @thockin

A few thoughts:

0) If, by chance, the hash ends up as 0 and we produce "" rather than "0", then that is a bug and should be fixed.

1) Regex parsing pod names to extract things like RS or deployment names IS NOT SUPPORTED.  We paused an effort to actively change this, because we don't want to break users, but it's already broken for very long names. If it works, it works by luck.  We should not endorse this pattern.

2) If doing this "right"  represents a real hardship for consumers, we should think up a better pattern that is more supportable. Please bring evidence. 

3) I am not against the idea of leading 0s, per se, but it has non-zero risk of breaking people who already parse this, and it sort of encourages this anti-best-practice of pattern matching. So I don't think it's worthwhile.

title: daemonset pod cannot be created quickly, when some nodes are added to the cluster and controller-manager OOM will be triggered
body:
### What happened? ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112319 【Question】 question 1: Now our k8s cluster has 5k nodes. When we expand some nodes in the k8s cluster, the daemonset pod cannot be created quickly. It takes about 2 hours to create the daemonset pod. Add a new node daemonset pod startup time: ![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/3377677/ef2d7885-1ce4-4e90-9340-205b00093f5f) ![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/3377677/5b0e4cb4-1fa2-470e-8eea-bb6e92c1002d) question 2: Look at the monitoring of `kube-controller-manager` Memory usage reaches 900GB and triggers OOM. `kube-controller-manager` memory usage monitoring: ![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/3377677/6b628b11-1676-4862-9616-07f99554ce36) 【Solution】 In a cluster with 5K nodes, we found that when the daemonset controller watches update `Node` events, due to the large number of `Node` events, the `NodeInformer` [pendingNotifications](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3e438c54a77ccf7b9e0aff924eb977031099cc2f/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L876) ring buffer has more `Node` events to be processed, resulting in the Node EventHandler's `Add/Update` callback function being processed slowly. Affects the creation of daemonset pod and `kube-controller-manager` `OOM` issues. We optimized the [shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1d9e1e6d56cbd5c9d04ba25cccf184a973056a79/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L693) logic in the [UpdateNode](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1d9e1e6d56cbd5c9d04ba25cccf184a973056a79/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L693) method of the daemonset controller `NodeInformer` to reduce unnecessary Node event processing: original code: ``` func shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate(oldNode, curNode v1.Node) bool { if !nodeInSameCondition(oldNode.Status.Conditions, curNode.Status.Conditions) { return false } oldNode.ResourceVersion = curNode.ResourceVersion oldNode.Status.Conditions = curNode.Status.Conditions return apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldNode, curNode) } ``` optimized code: ``` func shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate(oldNode, curNode v1.Node) bool { if !nodeInSameCondition(oldNode.Status.Conditions, curNode.Status.Conditions) { return false } oldNode.ResourceVersion = curNode.ResourceVersion oldNode.Status.Conditions = curNode.Status.Conditions + oldNode.Status.Images = curNode.Status.Images + oldNode.Status.NodeInfo = curNode.Status.NodeInfo + oldNode.Status.Capacity = curNode.Status.Capacity + oldNode.Status.Allocatable = curNode.Status.Allocatable return apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldNode, curNode) } func (dsc *DaemonSetsController) updateNode(old, cur interface{}) { oldNode := old.(*v1.Node) curNode := cur.(*v1.Node) + oldNodeCopy := oldNode.DeepCopy() + curNodeCopy := curNode.DeepCopy() if shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate(*oldNodeCopy, *curNodeCopy) { return } dsList, err := dsc.dsLister.List(labels.Everything()) if err != nil { klog.V(4).Infof("Error listing daemon sets: %v", err) return } // TODO: it'd be nice to pass a hint with these enqueues, so that each ds would only examine the added node (unless it has other work to do, too). for _, ds := range dsList { _, oldShouldSchedule, oldShouldContinueRunning, err := dsc.nodeShouldRunDaemonPod(oldNode, ds) if err != nil { klog.Errorf("Error old node %s should run daemon %s/%s pod: %v", oldNode.Name, ds.Namespace, ds.Name, err) continue } _, currentShouldSchedule, currentShouldContinueRunning, err := dsc.nodeShouldRunDaemonPod(curNode, ds) if err != nil { klog.Errorf("Error current node %s should run daemon %s/%s pod: %v", oldNode.Name, ds.Namespace, ds.Name, err) continue } if (oldShouldSchedule != currentShouldSchedule) || (oldShouldContinueRunning != currentShouldContinueRunning) { klog.V(4).Infof("enqueueing daemon set %s/%s for node %v.", ds.Namespace, ds.Name, curNode.Name) dsc.enqueueDaemonSet(ds) } } } ``` 【Effect】 After adding some nodes to the cluster, the daemonset pod can be quickly created, and the `kube-controller-manager` memory is controlled at about 20GB. ![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/3377677/5c9e3a0a-13ac-45c6-b722-d8a1c802b14b) ### What did you expect to happen? 1. When adding some nodes to the k8s cluster, daemonset pod can be created quickly because the node requires CNI daemonset pod. 2. kube-controller-manager needs to use less memory to prevent frequent `OOM`triggers. 3. We have optimized the `shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate` logic in the `updateNode` method of the daemonset controller `NodeInformer` to reduce unnecessary `Node `event processing. Is this optimization logic possible? ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? When the k8s cluster size reaches 5k, add new nodes to the cluster. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version

> 2. Excluding more things from the node comparison is one way to scope down `shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate`, but will definitely require copying the old node object, which is expensive to do. I _think_ the only things the daemonset controller pays attention to in the node are the 1) name, 2) labels, 3) taints. The name is immutable, so checking if the labels or taints changed seems like a cheaper way to implement `shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate`

@liggitt  Should we optimize `shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate` function and compare node labels and taints to solve this problem?
that would be my recommendation

I guess I have two thoughs - we should consider short-term mitigation and a medium-term fix:

1. For short-term mitigation, I agree with @liggitt - changing shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate to just compare labels & taints seems like a reasonable mitigation.

2. For medium-term mitigation, we should rewrite the controller to the pattern where event-handler is as cheap as possible by simply putting stuff into queue. The queue then gives us deduplication for free and all the logic is then happening in the workers.

Possibly this is just logger indeed. Still it is important imo because it makes looking for real panics in logs hard. This was my use case to understand another issue.

The logger sees an `any` (= `interface{}`) value which implements `fmt.Stringer` and calls it's `String` method - in this case, https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.21.3:src/time/format.go;l=527. That then panics.

We've gone back and forth whether the logging call should try to call the `String` method and recover from a panic or try to do some advance checks whether the `any` value is perhaps nil. There could be `String` implementations for pointers which produce some nice output for `nil`, so not calling it would be a loss. Also, detecting nil values is surprisingly hard, if I remember correctly (the `fmt.Stringer` interface is non-nil, only the value hidden inside it is)), therefore currently the code simply calls it.

```
datalake   ExternalName   <none>        minio.datalake.svc.cluster.local   <none>    5m54s
minio      ClusterIP      10.0.142.29   <none>                             80/TCP    6m46s
trino      ClusterIP      10.0.153.81   <none>                             80/TCP    6m52s

$ k -n datalake run "test-$RANDOM" -ti --restart=Never --image=busybox cat /etc/resolv.conf
search datalake.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local us-central1-b.c.thockin-dev.internal c.thockin-dev.internal google.internal
nameserver 10.0.0.10
options ndots:5

$ k -n datalake run "test-$RANDOM" -ti --restart=Never --image=thockin/dnsutils -- dig +search +short trino.datalake.svc.cluster.local
10.0.153.81

$ k -n datalake run "test-$RANDOM" -ti --restart=Never --image=thockin/dnsutils -- dig +search +short trino.datalake.svc
10.0.153.81

$ k -n datalake run "test-$RANDOM" -ti --restart=Never --image=thockin/dnsutils -- dig +search +short trino.datalake
minio.datalake.svc.cluster.local.
10.0.142.29
```

So you can see this is reproducible.  For completeness, the shortest name works:

```
$ k -n datalake run "test-$RANDOM" -ti --restart=Never --image=thockin/dnsutils -- dig +search +short trino
10.0.153.81
```

And the "problem" name works from another namespace:

```
$ k -n default run "test-$RANDOM" -ti --restart=Never --image=thockin/dnsutils -- dig +search +short trino.datalake
10.0.153.81
```

So the issue is that WITHIN THAT NAMESPACE, your query is ambiguous (sorry!)

By default, all names are subject to search-path expansion.  Unless you configure otherwise, that means:
1) `<query>.<this-namespace>.svc.<zone>`
2) `<query>.svc.<zone>`
3) `<query>.<zone>`
4) `<query>`

You seem to want `trino.datalake` to skip (1) and hit (2), but I think it will actually hit (1), because `<host>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.<suffix>` is a valid query, and seems to be matching

```
$ k -n datalake run "test-$RANDOM" -ti --restart=Never --image=thockin/dnsutils -- dig +search +showsearch +nocomments trino.datalake

; <<>> DiG 9.18.19-1~deb12u1-Debian <<>> +search +showsearch +nocomments trino.datalake
;; global options: +cmd
;trino.datalake.datalake.svc.cluster.local. IN A
trino.datalake.datalake.svc.cluster.local. 30 IN CNAME minio.datalake.svc.cluster.local.
minio.datalake.svc.cluster.local. 30 IN	A	10.0.142.29
;; Query time: 1 msec
;; SERVER: 10.0.0.10#53(10.0.0.10) (UDP)
;; WHEN: Thu Feb 01 19:47:22 UTC 2024
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 217
```

Note the DNS question is "trino.datalake.datalake.svc.cluster.local." which is being satisfied by the CNAME (external-name) for datalake.datalake.svc.cluster.local.

But why?  Let's look at the spec: https://github.com/kubernetes/dns/blob/master/docs/specification.md#25---records-for-external-name-services

It actually only specifies a CNAME record for  `<service>.<ns>.svc.<zone>.`  To my eyes, that SHOULD NOT match, but CNAMEs have sometimes surprising semantics.

@chrisohaver - can you shed some light, maybe?
This errant behavior was fixed in https://github.com/coredns/coredns/pull/6162 and should be in the latest coredns release 1.11.1
YAY!

title: Kubelet didn't respect --resolv-conf when resolv.conf is empty or full of comments
body:
### What happened?

When I passing `--resolv-conf` to kubelet, it did not respect the option, and still copy the `/etc/resolv.conf` to the pod.

What makes it special is that the `resolv.conf` provided by myself is empty.

> https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/

After skimming the code, I found the logic here is problematic:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.2/pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go#L225-L274

Because `resolv.conf` is empty, an empty array and no error is returned. Then, if the dnsPolicy is `default` (that is the default config for CoreDNS deployment), the `podDNSType` turns to be `podDNSHost`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.2/pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go#L316-L317

Then, containerd will get an empty `dns_config`, so it will copy `/etc/resolv.conf` from the host to the container:

https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/v1.7.6/pkg/cri/server/sandbox_run_linux.go#L282-L287

Finally, CoreDNS reports forwarding loop error.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should refuse to use the wrong empty `resolv.conf` to create a pod, and complains with errors.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Pass `--resolv-conf` to kubelet, and make sure the specified `resolv.conf` file is empty.
2. Check the output of CoreDNS, and its `/etc/resolv.conf`.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

This situation MAY occur when systemd-resolved is used, and the operator pass the `--resolv-conf /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` to kubelet. 

Although systemd-resolved create this file in manner of "create temp, write temp, rename" ...

This is a fun bug, but not that hard to comprehend, I think.

Forget whether it's a "good idea" or not.

Is it valid to pass an empty file to `--resolv-conf` ?  If yes, should it mean the same as not passing that flag or should it mean "no config".

I think it IS valid and it SHOULD mean "no config".  What really happens is that kubelet gets empty slices (but no error, so not ambiguous).  When it creates the DNSConfig message,  it appears empty, because it is comprised entirely of `repeated` fields with no instances.  That is ambiguous - it could mean "no data" or "not specified".  It's unclear to me if we can tell the difference between those?  @samuelkarp @SergeyKanzhelev @ndixita - do you know?  `PodSandboxConfig.GetDnsConfig()` *can* return nil.

Containerd further conflates those two by parsing into a string, and assuming `""` means "not specified".  Even if it WAS specified!

Then, containerd "helpfully" decides that, if you don't specify any contents, it should copy the host's resolv.conf.
 
I am not 100% confident in CRI semantics - is it valid for CRI to NOT populate the `PodSandboxConfig.DNSConfig` message?  Or is that effectively required?  If a CRI caller does not specify `PodSandboxConfig.DNSConfig`, is the CORRECT behavior to go look at the host?  That seems like over-stepping, to me.  If I wanted a DNS config, I would have sent it.  Agree or disagree?

So IMO, the fix here is either (in my pref order):

1) containerd should not fall back on host's resolv.conf AT ALL
2) containerd should differentiate "not provided" from "provided and empty" (`PodSandboxConfig.GetDnsConfig()` returned nil)
3) we should add a "this struct intentionally left blank" marker to `DNSConfig`, so containerd can do the above

So I think this very much *is* a SIG Node issue.

/sig node

As to the question of how this problem was discovered....why are you setting the kubelet to an empty resolv.conf rather than just configuring the specific Pods in question?
https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/9730

> As to the question of how this problem was discovered....why are you setting the kubelet to an empty resolv.conf rather than just configuring the specific Pods in question?

@thockin This is because CoreDNS reports a forwarding loop issue due to systemd-resolved is used in the node, and I pass `--resolv-conf /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` to kubelet. But it has a race condition here when the node restarted, the file may be full of comments if there is no available name server at the time.

And after a while, systemd-resolved got an available dns server by any way, then the UPLINK config should be recreated, however the kubelet have taken the stale and full-of-comments `/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf`.

Of course passing an empty `--resolv-conf` is incorrect, but it is not deliberately.
Fixed in containerd

> [containerd/containerd#9730](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/9730)

@saschagrunert @haircommander @mrunalp you should check if you need to fix this too in cri-o ^^^

It looks like [`cri-o/cri-o`](https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/main/internal/factory/sandbox/infra.go#L89-L93) does nothing if `DNSConfig` is nil. Only in case of an empty struct of `DSNConfig` `/etc/resolv.conf` [be copied](https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/main/internal/factory/sandbox/infra.go#L128-L130).


I'm going to create a PR in `cri-o`.
Thank you @roman-kiselenko and thanks @aojea for the hint! :heart:

title: Flag to Disable the 6-minute Force Detach Window
body:
### What happened?

Certain online upgrade workflows might need to restart kubernetes as a part of their upgrade procedure. This can lead to the following sequence:
* As a part of draining a kubernetes node, a pod might get deleted.
* The unmount of a pod could take more than 6 minutes.
* If the node is deemed unhealthy when the 6 minute timer fires for the pod being deleted (for example, because kubelet is still restarting), then the underlying PV will be force detached (via a `ControllerUnpublishVolume` RPC)

These workflows would likely benefit from disabling this feature in lieu of the Non-Graceful Node Shutdown feature that hit GA in kubernetes 1.28 (see [here](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/) for more details).

When these issues are encountered in our testbeds, we are left with Zombie iSCSI LUNs. If pods end up migrating to a node with such a Zombie LUN present, those pods might end up attaching themselves to the Zombie LUN leading to data corruption.

This data corruption has caused a number of our cluster-management applications to lose all access to their data, requiring them to be deployed from scratch (occasionally causing downtime for the entire cluster).

### What did you expect to happen?

The ControllerUnpublishVolume request to wait indefinitely until NodeUnstageVolume has succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See the “What happened?” section for more details.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

/sig Storage

Tagging @bswartz, @msau42, @saad-ali, @jingxu97

Hi @rohitssingh 

Thank you for the detailed issue report. The issue you've described with zombie iSCSI LUNs during Kubernetes upgrades sounds concerning, especially with the data corruption implications for cluster-management applications.

Firstly, I noticed there's a version skew between your client (1.23) and server (1.27) that exceeds the supported minor version skew of +/-1. While this may not be directly related to the issue you're facing, it's generally a good idea to align the versions for more consistent behavior.

Regarding the ControllerUnpublishVolume behavior, the intent of the 6-minute timer was to provide a timeout for certain scenarios, but it seems that in your case, it leads to undesirable outcomes. Since Kubernetes 1.28 introduced the Non-Graceful Node Shutdown feature, you're correct that disabling the previous timer-based feature could be beneficial.

Possible Solutions and Next Steps:
Upgrade to Kubernetes 1.28 or later: If possible, consider upgrading your Kubernetes cluster to take advantage of the Non-Graceful Node Shutdown feature.

Further Investigation: We would like to reproduce this issue in a controlled environment to understand it better. Would you be willing to share additional logs that could be useful?

Temporary Workaround: As an immediate workaround, you may consider scripting a manual detach procedure that accounts for the time needed for NodeUnstageVolume to succeed.

We'll be looking into this issue more thoroughly. I'll keep you updated on our findings and potential fixes.

Thanks again for bringing this to our attention. Your detailed explanation is invaluable in understanding the severity and specifics of the problem.

Our issue was specific to the protocol we were using (iSCSI). Specifically, the problem was that the storage controller thought a LUN id was free for use (because of ControllerUnpublishVolume) when in fact it was still in use by a k8s node.

To reproduce this issue, I would suggest that you:
* Inject errors in the NodeUnstageVolume path for a particular LUN.
* Cordon the node that is running a pod that uses said LUN.
* Delete the pod that was using that LUN.
* The pod should try to come up on another node, leaving a "zombie" device behind.

If you then uncordon the node in question and cordon all other nodes and then start creating new pods that use new PVs, eventually the underlying storage controller will re-use the LUN id that was used by the "zombie" device; the LUN that comes up with this id will be in the state I mentioned above.

I hope that helps!

Or in some weird way the other "new" LUNs get corrupted?

> Thanks! just to make sure, the original LUN from the pod is the one getting corrupted? So the data of the original application?
> 
> Or in some weird way the other "new" LUNs get corrupted?

There are two cases to consider:
1) In the situation where the storage system can reuse the same LUN number for two different volumes, the main worry is that the new LUN gets confused with the old LUN, and the new LUN gets corrupted because it's mapped to a LUN number that the node things belongs to the old volume. In this case the old volume is safe, having been detached, and the risk comes from the confusion caused by reuse of numbers.
2) You can have a case when the volume gets detached after 6 minutes, and attached to another node, then later detached and reattached back to the original node. Since the node doesn't know that another node has mounted/unmounted the volume in the meantime, it may think it's had exclusive access all long and will flush dirty buffers to the disk once it regains access. This would corrupt the original volume.

Both problems stem from the lack of node-side cleanup when the 6-minute force detach triggers. For this reason the only safe thing to do is to disable the 6-minute timer, and handle dead nodes by actually rebooting them and tainting the node.
