The worst case I encountered was actually a combination of the two cases that Ben mentioned.

Let us say that we have two volumes in use by two different pods:
```
V in use by pod p
W in use by pod q
```

And two k8s hosts:
```
N
O
```

Along with three random LUN ids:
```
i
j
k
```

Let us assume that our LUN mappings are unique to each k8s host.

If initially `V` is mapped to `N` @ `i`, we will have the following LUN mappings:

```
On k8s Hosts			On the Storage Controllers
============			==========================
N:
i -> V					i -> V 

O:
N/A						N/A
```

This looks fine so far.

But things can get broken if we try to migrate pod `p`, which uses `V`, to `O`.

Node N has 6 minutes to tear down `V` so that it can be resurrected on `O`. However, if the timer fires before cleanup finishes, then KCM will prematurely issue a `ControllerUnpublishVolume` leading to a force detach.

This will leave us with:
```
On k8s Hosts			On the Storage Controllers
============			==========================
N:
i -> V					N/A

O:
N/A						N/A
```

Later, KCM will issue a `ControllerPublishVolume` for `V` on `O`, leaving:
```
On k8s Hosts			On the Storage Controllers
============			==========================
N:
i -> V					N/A

O:
j -> V					j -> V 
```

where `j` is some LUN id that was free for use in `O`'s mapping space.

The state on node `N` is not correct and can now result in serious problems after more pods get scheduled. Among other issues, this is dangerous because all of `V`'s buffers might not be flushed and committed at the time the mapping is broken. But as we will see, we have bigger problems too...

If pod `q` now gets scheduled on `N`, the storage controller is free to allocate any available LUN id; since it believes `i` is available, it is free to use it again.

If it does opt to allocate `i` here, we will then have the following mappings:
```
On k8s Hosts			On the Storage Controllers
============			==========================
N:
i -> V					N/A
i -> W					i -> W

O:
j -> V					j -> V 
```

Technically speaking, we do not yet have an problem; though we have a stale mapping for `V` on `N`, it is not actively in use.

But we will have a problem if `p` ever returns to `N`, when we will have:
```
On k8s Hosts			On the Storage Controllers
============			==========================
N:
i -> V					k -> V
i -> W					i -> W

O:
N/A						N/A
```

where `k` is some LUN id that was free for use in `N`'s mapping space.

Since the device is already established (and maybe even mounted in the appropriate namespace), the underlying machinery will then present the same LUN (i.e., `i` which is actually mapped to the LUN backing `W`) to both pods `p` & `q`. This will result in data corruption as both pods proceed to write data & flush their respective superblocks.

I will let Ben speak to the driver-side mitigations (in particular, the change you referenced seems to be his handiwork :) ).

> Is the existence of these dirty buffers realistic in a k8s environment? Where would dirty data come from? the first iteration of the workload (on this node?) Is that even possible?

Rohit gave a very detailed explanation, but very shortly, the dirty data is any data written by an application or filesystem which never got acknowledged because write access was cut off by a controller unpublish. This can happen if you trigger the non-graceful-node-shutdown feature _without_ actually rebooting the node. Once the node regains write access to the volume it will continue writing without checking to see if anyone else wrote data in the mean time.

> Another question, I saw some drivers implementing guard rails (for what it looks like) against this problem: [NetApp/trident@b33021d](https://github.com/NetApp/trident/commit/b33021d64da7588d65b7f38cda7cd01873850e14) (Second point) I guess those guard rails make sense regardless of the force detach behavior, since any bug in the driver could lead to a "force detach". WDYT?

I have never successfully used the Trident force detach feature. I know that it's one of many such implementations in drivers to try to mitigate this problem. How easy or hard this is depends a lot of the underlying data protocol. iSCSI is one of the worst I've seen, thanks to how complex the Linux initiator implemenation is.

Thanks again for investing in replies here @rohitssingh @bswartz!
I have tried to follow the reproducer;

> If pod `q` now gets scheduled on `N`, the storage controller is free to allocate any available LUN id; since it believes `i` is available, it is free to use it again.
> 
> If it does opt to allocate `i` here, we will then have the following mappings:
> 
> ```
> On k8s Hosts			On the Storage Controllers
> ============			==========================
> N:
> i -> V					N/A
> i -> W					i -> W
> 
> O:
> j -> V					j -> V 
> ```
> 
> Technically speaking, we do not yet have an problem; though we have a stale mapping for `V` on `N`, it is not actively in use.

Thing is, at least with multipath, it will correct this state once a new volume/pod combo schedules on `N`.
So, I am seeing that it **does** opt to allocate LUN ID `i`, it just remediates the force detached state as far as `lsblk/multipath -ll` is concerned - the "bad" entry disappears from `multipath -ll` output.
So I don't think is the case for me
> ```
> On k8s Hosts			On the Storage Controllers
> ============			==========================
> N:
> i -> V					N/A
> ```
and instead it's
> ```
> On k8s Hosts			On the Storage Controllers
> ============			==========================
> N:
> i -> W					i -> W
> ```

And thus upon completing the reproducer's execution, I see no corruption.
I think these multipath logs are related to the remediation
```
multipathd[32318]: sdc: path wwid changed from 'FORCE_DETACHED_WWID' to 'NEW_WWID'
...
multipathd[32318]: 8:32: path removed from map FORCE_DETACHED_WWID
multipathd[32318]: FORCE_DETACHED_WWID: sdd - tur checker reports path is up
multipathd[32318]: FORCE_DETACHED_WWID: remaining active paths: 1
multipathd[32318]: sdd: path wwid changed from 'FORCE_DETACHED_WWID' to 'NEW_WWID'
multipathd[32318]: FORCE_DETACHED_WWID Last path deleted, disabling queueing
multipathd[32318]: FORCE_DETACHED_WWID: map flushed after removing all paths
```

Were you encountering the issues on an environment with multipath as well?

@rohitssingh this log message:
```
multipathd[32318]: FORCE_DETACHED_WWID Last path deleted, disabling queueing
```
means `flush_on_last_del` is enabled and it disabled `queue_if_no_path` when the last path was deleted.

@akalenyu  looking at those logs, it looks like they are already consistent with a situation where corruption can occur. These two lines:
```
multipathd[32318]: FORCE_DETACHED_WWID: sdd - tur checker reports path is up
multipathd[32318]: FORCE_DETACHED_WWID: remaining active paths: 1
```
are printed by the path checker. Specifically `remaining active paths` is printed after the path is re-enabled. The line where the changed WWID is noticed:
```
multipathd[32318]: sdd: path wwid changed from 'FORCE_DETACHED_WWID' to 'NEW_WWID'
```
is printed when multipathd processes the uevent that presumably was issued when the LUN reappeared, and it appears after the path checker lines. The moment that the path is re-enabled in the kernel, it is able to flush any queued IO to it. This means that if there was queued IO to that device, these logs appear to show a window where the kernel could have sent it to the bad path before multipathd removed it. It is possible to close this window by setting the `recheck_wwid` configuration parameter. This will check for changed WWIDs whenever a path comes back online. That still can't remove the possibility of corruption completely. It is possible that a path changes WWIDs without multipathd ever noticing that it went down, and IO could go to it before multipathd processes the uevent for the change.

nodes.title: Add a flag to disable force detach behavior in kube-controller-manager
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR adds a flag to allow the 6-minute force detach window to be disabled.

With this flag enabled, `ControllerUnpublishVolume` RPCs will not be dispatched if a given pod is stuck unmounting for 6-minutes and the node is deemed to be Unhealthy in that window.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #120328

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
This change adds the following CLI option for `kube-controller-manager`:
* `disable-force-detach` (defaults to `false`): Prevent force detaching volumes based on maximum unmount time and node status. If enabled, the non-graceful node shutdown feature must be used to recover from node failure (see https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/). If enabled and a pod must be forcibly terminated at the risk of corruption, then the appropriate VolumeAttachment object (see here: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/volume-attachment-v1/) must be deleted.
```

title: Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.
body:
### What happened?

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L984-L1006
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). It will update the **allocatedDevices** map of ManagerImpl, because of mutex is unlock by step 1. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L519-L543
4.  Kubelet continues with the first pod. If **allocatedDevices** has changed and GPU device is nil, kubelet will panic in the closure allocateRemainingFrom.

In our observation, right after deleting the pod, the podresources API was called. This removed the state of `allocatedDevices` for the GPU resource. This happened when the `UpdateAllocatedDevices` was called as soon as the mutex got unlocked in the `callGetPreferredAllocationIfAvailable`.
Moreover, such a race seems being triggered when Device Plugin periodically calls podresources API.

This happened when the `UpdateAllocatedDevices` was called as soon as the mutex got unlocked in the `callGetPreferredAllocationIfAvailable`. Moreover, such a race seems being triggered when Device Plugin periodically calls podresources API.

Thanks, this information matches with other findings. The podresources endpoint intentionally triggers `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to report the current up to date allocation; otherwise the device manager would clean up lazily the allocation state when a new admission is attempted.
We will work on a fix.

When a pod completes, the scheduler moves all the pending pods back into the active/backoff.

title: Deletion of pod with prestop hook takes longer than expected.
body:
### What happened?

Deletion of pod with prestop hook takes longer than expected.

The logic of deleting a Pod is implemented through the `kubelet.killPod(pod, gracePeriodOverride)`, which is responsible for deleting all the of the pod container, including concurrently executing `PrestopHook` and `StopContainer`, as well as finally stopping the Sandbox. 

Initially, the `gracePeriodOverride` parameter was only used to override the graceful shutdown duration of `StopContainer` in the CRI interface. Only in some special cases (such as eviction, shutdown node, etc.) would this parameter be used. 

If the timeout parameter in StopContainer was not overridden, it would be `timeout = max(2s, pod.spec.TerminationGracePeriodSeconds - PrestopHookPeriod)`. 

After kubelet 1.22, `pod.spec.TerminationGracePeriodSeconds` is passed as a parameter to `kubelet.killPod` when calling kubelet.killPod, causing `StopContainer` to continue to use the full graceful shutdown duration of the pod instead of the remaining duration.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dea1312e03a0d6b7bc73ff21fa243cccea419c76/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#LL907C26-L907C26

**_This means that in kubelet 1.20 and below, assuming the pod.spec.TerminationGracePeriodSeconds is set to 120 seconds and the prestop executes a sleep for 50 seconds, the time left for `StopContainer` is 70 seconds. But in kubelet 1.22 and above, assuming the pod.spec.TerminationGracePeriodSeconds is set to 120 seconds and the prestop executes a sleep for 50 seconds, the graceful shutdown time left for the container is still 120 seconds._** 

This conflicts with the docs https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/#hook-handler-execution.

### What did you expect to happen?

I want to know whether it is a code problem or a document problem. 

And may I submit a PR for this.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Change kubelet parameter --v=4.
2. Create pod as following.
3. `kubectl delete pod <pod name>`

``` yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - sleep
    - "10000"
    image: ubuntu:latest
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command:
          - sleep
          - "10"
    name: sleep
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 20
```

We'll got
```

title: Grace Termination Period timer doesn't start before preStop
body:
### What happened?

Implementing graceful shutdown by leveraging `preStop` hooks. According to all the documentation I can find the `terminatinoGracePeriodSeconds` includes the time that the `preStop` is running, meaning the timer starts before `preStop` executes.

In my setup I have a simple `preStop` that sleeps for 15 seconds. In my app code I then sleep for 90 seconds in the SIGTERM handler. Given that the default terminationGracePeriod is 30 seconds I would expect that the POD is killed 15 seconds after the SIGTERM handler reports it received the signal. However the POD receives the SIGTERM (prints out that it did) and then lives for a while 30 seconds after that point. 

### What did you expect to happen?

As it states here:

* https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/
* https://www.datree.io/resources/kubernetes-guide-graceful-shutdown-with-lifecycle-prestop-hook#anchor5
* https://livebook.manning.com/concept/kubernetes/terminationgraceperiodsecond

```
The Pod's termination grace period countdown begins before the PreStop hook is executed, so regardless of the outcome of the handler, the container will eventually terminate within the Pod's termination grace period.
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I have the following simple NodeJS app:

```
import * as Koa from 'koa';
import * as Router from 'koa-router';

const app = new Koa();
const router = new Router();

function delay(time) {
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, time));
}

router.get("/", ctx => {
  ctx.body = 'Hello World';
});

app.use(router.routes);
app.use(router.allowedMethods());

export const server = app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log(`Server listening on port 3000`);
});

process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  server.close(async() => {
    console.log('Received SIGTERM, closing server');
    await delay(90000);
  });
});
```

As you can see in the SIGTERM handler it prints out the signal was received and then simply sleeps for 90 seconds.

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: debug
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: debug
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: debug
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: debug
    spec:
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: dockerconfigjson-jfrog
      containers:
      - name: node
        image: test:latest
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command:
                - sleep
                - "15"
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: 128Mi
          limits:
            memory: 256Mi
```

My deployment of above code adds a preStop that simply sleeps for 15 seconds. 

When I delete this POD, the application receives the SIGTERM after 15 seconds (as expected). It then lives for a whole 30 more seconds before being forcefully terminated. Give that the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is set to 30 seconds if I am interpreting the documentation above correctly the POD should have been forcefully terminated at 15 seconds after receiving SIGTERM.

```
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command:
          - sleep
          - "15"
    name: node
    resources:
      limits:
        memory: 256Mi
      requests:
        memory: 128Mi
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  serviceAccount: default
  serviceAccountName: default
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

```

title: [scheduling] movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue moves wrong pods to active or backoff queue
body:
### What happened?

In movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue function, we will move pods in podInfoList to Active or Backoff queue, and then we set moveRequestCycle as current schedulingCycle. Setting moveRequestCycle will reschedule the pod currently being scheduled.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L770

Sometimes, when AssignedPodAdded is triggered, we will call movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue, event if the pod currently being scheduled is unrelated to the newly assignedPod, it will be recheduled.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L712


### What did you expect to happen?

Should we reschedule the current pod only when the currently scheduled pod is related to an event?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Submit a pod with nodename when scheduler is scheduling another pod.

_No response_

The pod being attempted in the current scheduling cycle will either be added to the backoff or the unschedulable queue if the attempt fails: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L519

Are you suggesting that it should always be added to unschedulablePods? if so, that doesn't sound right because the cluster state changed in a way that may make it schedulable and we should attempt it again.

Hi, thanks for your time! @ahg-g  

> Are you suggesting that it should always be added to unschedulablePods? if so, that doesn't sound right because the cluster state changed in a way that may make it schedulable and we should attempt it again.

No, I am talking about another case. 
For example, one pod A is in scheduling cycle and another pod B is bound to a node this time. Then the scheduler will get a `assignedPodAdded` event, this event will trigger `movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1f901acf44f8adf69759db434690c2a8bdd616b/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L710-L714
and in movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue we will always set `p.moveRequestCycle = p.schedulingCycle`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1f901acf44f8adf69759db434690c2a8bdd616b/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L768-L801
Even `p.getUnschedulablePodsWithMatchingAffinityTerm(pod)` return empty set, we set `p.moveRequestCycle = p.schedulingCycle`, which will reschedule pod A. And in most time we are not have to reschedule it. 
Maybe we should do some check when we set `p.moveRequestCycle = p.schedulingCycle`. WDYT?
I don't know if I explain it clearly. Please ask me if you have any question.

In the scenario you mentioned pod A will end up in one of two states: 
1. if the scheduling cycle matched it with a node, it will be bound to the node
2. if the scheduling cycle failed to find a matching node, it will be placed in the backoff queue

I don't understand what you mean by "which will reschedule pod A", is it different from the behavior I am describing above?

> I don't understand what you mean by "which will reschedule pod A", is it different from the behavior I am describing above?

I mean, some event won't make pod schedulable, maybe we need to check it before set `moveRequestCycle`. Like:

```
if isEventMayMakeCurrentPodSchedulable() {
 	p.moveRequestCycle = p.schedulingCycle 
}
```

title: cronjob controller: reconsider log verbosity
body:
### What happened?

We are running Kubernetes 1.25.5 and trying to configure kube-controller-manager to be less verbose when logging.
We run kube-controller-manager as a static pod created by Kubelet and use the following command where we pass `--v=0`:
```
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-controller-manager
    - --feature-gates=EphemeralContainers=true,TopologyAwareHints=true
    - --allocate-node-cidrs=true
    - --authentication-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --authorization-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --cluster-cidr=10.6.0.0/16
    - --configure-cloud-routes=false
    - --kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --leader-elect=true
    - --node-monitor-grace-period=120s
    - --root-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/ca.pem
    - --service-account-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/signing-key.pem
    - --use-service-account-credentials
    - --v=0
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.25.5
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    livenessProbe:
      failureThreshold: 3
      httpGet:
        host: 127.0.0.1
        path: /healthz
        port: 10257
        scheme: HTTPS
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 15
    name: kube-controller-manager
```
The `--v=0` flag seems to passed fine to the final command line of kube-controller-manager:
```
root     2464651  285  1.6 1939088 1085624 ?     Ssl  05:59 544:37 kube-controller-manager --feature-gates=EphemeralContainers=true,TopologyAwareHints=true --allocate-node-cidrs=true --authentication-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf --authorization-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf --cluster-cidr=10.6.0.0/16 --configure-cloud-routes=false --kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf --leader-elect=true --node-monitor-grace-period=120s --root-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/ca.pem --service-account-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/signing-key.pem --use-service-account-credentials --v=0
```

Even though we get tons of the following logs periodically:
```
kube-controller-manager-master-2.dev.merit.uw.systems kube-controller-manager I0202 06:52:05.808355       1 event.go:294] "Event occurred" object="energy/gba-fabricator-job" fieldPath="" kind="CronJob" apiVersion="batch/v1" type="Normal" reason="JobAlreadyActive" message="Not starting job because prior execution is running and concurrency policy is Forbid"
```
which come from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L575 where is logged as klog.V(4).InfoS
So arguably this line should not appear on our controller logs.

### What did you expect to happen?

Setting flag `--v=0` should be enough to lower log verbosity level according to: https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Scheduling a long running job at small intervals should be enough to reproduce our exact case and get the above mentioned logs.

### Anything else we need to know?

@ffilippopoulos you are referring to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/70dde8d746a07392d945dde32dd7e3b12ca9a043/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L575
when you refer to 
`
where is logged as klog.V(4).InfoS
So arguably this line should not appear on our controller logs.
`
but the message you are getting is from

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/70dde8d746a07392d945dde32dd7e3b12ca9a043/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L576

I could be wrong here

@RayAsh37: well spotted.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/70dde8d746a07392d945dde32dd7e3b12ca9a043/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/record/event.go#L307 prints the log message with a verbosity of 0 as determined by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L131

Whether events should be logged at that verbosity I don't know. The `klog.V(4).InfoS` calls before each `jm.recorder.Eventf` also seem redundant.

/unassign
/retitle cronjob controller: reconsider log verbosity
Ok, I assumed that I am seeing the message from `klog` as I wasn't aware that `jm.recorder.Eventf` will also result in printing log messages. So there is no way to avoid getting this for now?
Not without modifying the source code of the cronjob controller.

```
	// Start event processing pipeline.
	jm.broadcaster.StartStructuredLogging(0)
```
Is the verbosity `0` as the log level that events are logged too low as suggested by [sig instrumentation](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md#what-method-to-use)? 
Users cannot ignore event messages by lowering the log level. It causes information noise.

I think we can increase this value or make it changeable. 
for example: [kubelet sets this event verbosity to 3](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5690f12b69aac5ab4eb0e226682ef68b4059d6e/cmd/kubelet/app/server.go#L514)
What do you think? @kow3ns @janetkuo @soltysh @smarterclayton @pohly
Makes sense to me.

I traced it down to this change https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/91712 and most controllers are doing `StartStructuredLogging(0)`. I'm fine with increasing the log level to be >0, following the recommendation from SIG instrumentation. Ideally it should be done for all controllers.

I don't think that SIG instrumentation has recommendations for this particular case. Also note that https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/91712 didn't change the verbosity of these events, they were at "info" (v=0) level already before in kube-controller-manager.

It's under the purvey of the individual code owners how important these events are, except that here we probably want consistency inside kube-controller-manager, so this probably should go to SIG Apps.

FWIW, logging at level 3 makes more sense to me than the current level 0.

/remove-sig instrumentation
/sig apps

Looking at this issue more in depth there are 2 things that I'd like to see being resolved:
1. Increasing the global level for broadcaster's logging to 3, such that this is the new base line. See [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1f3256bbac668f120433990028ca1fe206e4117b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/record/event.go#L368-L372) for more details.
2. Making sure the context is properly injected into the broadcaster, this will allow the `-v` flag value to be used also in that broadcaster, rather than the above global value. Again see [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1f3256bbac668f120433990028ca1fe206e4117b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/record/event.go#L368-L372) for explanation.

In other words, looking at cronjob controller we need:
1. [this line](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1f3256bbac668f120433990028ca1fe206e4117b/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L132) needs to look like: 
```golang
jm.broadcaster.StartStructuredLogging(3)
```
2. [this line](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1f3256bbac668f120433990028ca1fe206e4117b/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L85) need to look like:
```golang
eventBroadcaster := record.NewBroadcaster(record.WithContext(ctx))
```

This should be applied consistently to all controllers. @mengjiao-liu since you're bringing this over to sig-apps call, are you interested in working on this?

/assign

Thanks for the reply.  I will work on this.
@mengjiao-liu once you have a PR up and ready for review, please ping me directly on slack to get a faster response. Thank you!

title: Aggregated Discovery doesn't show aggregated apiservices as Stale before initial health check
body:
### What happened?

[Quote from KEP 3352](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/3352-aggregated-discovery#aggregation):

> A post start hook will be added and the kube-apiserver health check should only pass if the discovery document is ready. Since aggregated api servers may take longer to respond and we do not want to delay cluster startup, the health check will only block on the local api servers (built-ins and CRDs) to have their discovery ready. For api servers that have not been aggregated, their group-versions will be published with an empty resource list and a Stale for Freshness to indicate that they have not synced yet.

This requirement is not met. Explanation in first comment shows we wait for local services to sync before health check, but we do not include aggregated apiservices that had not yet synced as Stale.

I think for this one we almost have all our bases covered. For context, there is a single `AggregatedDiscoveryGroupManager` used by all of apiserver, apiextensions-apiserver, and aggregated-apiserver:

It is attached to genericConfig and the instance is shared by all three genericapiserver instances.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/201caf28b270d73c31b4f1f358548b1be608446c/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L477-L479

For builtin types, the `genericapiserver` adds its types directly during initialization to the shared `AggregatedDiscoveryGroupManager ` when installing APIs, so there is no need to wait in a post-start hook for builtins:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/201caf28b270d73c31b4f1f358548b1be608446c/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver.go#L706-L712

For CRDs there is a post-start hook to wait for discovery controller to sync initial list of CRDs. This uses the same `AggregatedDiscoveryGroupManager` instance used by genericapiserver.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/60d73ba75148483d150622a4d8b6e122e189ceab/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/apiserver.go#L213

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/60d73ba75148483d150622a4d8b6e122e189ceab/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/apiserver.go#L250-L255

Aggregated APIServer also uses the same `DiscoveryResourceManager` and is not responsible for syncing any local APIServices.

The only thing missing from this requirement is that aggregated APIServices are not present in the initial document as `Stale`.

@alexzielenski please correct me if I'm missing something but isn't the purpose of `dirtyAPIServiceQueue` [field](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed98c1da6d5fd1382a97663038c0fedbc02ebf9f/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apiserver/handler_discovery.go#L85) already adding APIServices as Stale?.

You summarized code navigation pretty well above, I started looking at the issue in case I can fix it, but I couldn't find the bug :)

Not sure if this was addressed but I'm going to make a pass on this and make sure it's fixed for GA.

/assign

@alexzielenski what do we want to the limit the cache size by?
the cache currently doesn't purge `serviceKey`s which are not being used by an `apiService`
is this still an issue? should it be resolved before enabling by default?

> is this still an issue? should it be resolved before enabling by default?

Can you elaborate? I am not sure what you mean by enabling by default?

> is this still an issue? 

Yes

> should it be resolved before enabling by default?

That's the cache for the downloaded discovery for each apiservice. The list probably doesn't grow very large. Fix is in #116828. Considering the pain of non-aggregated discovery on some users, and the time they have had to wait to get the feature, I'd say the trade-off is that this isn't nearly as bad.

It's also worth noting that the cache should only grow for Aggregated APIServices that themselves expose aggregated discovery endpoint. We don't store a cache entry here otherwise. The list doesn't grow unless the aggregated discovery document was successfully fetched.

This is a very rare case and especially at release a minuscule number of people on the bleeding edge might run into it. And even then it is not likely to be changing the `Spec.Service` so often once it is working enough to store a cache entry.

title: [Winkernel Proxier] Unexpected active TCP connection drops while horizontally scaling the endpoints for a LoadBalancer Service with External Traffic Policy: Local
body:
### What happened?

On a service of type LoadBalancer with External Traffic Policy: Local, whenever pod restarts other pods within the same Service stop responding to active connections from the Clients.


1. N clients are connected to M pods somewhat evenly, there are N established TCP connections.
2. One particular pod P is manually restarted/deleted.
3. Multiple(N/M) clients which are currently connected to P start seeing drops on Active connections, which is somewhat expected.
5. But the remaining (N-N/M) connections between clients and the other pods are negatively affected and some of them break.

For example if a deployment has pods 1,2,3,4,5. Each pod has TCP sessions where clients are connected and sending data. If pod 4 goes down some of the other pods 1,2,3,5 have their existing connections affected by pod 4 going down.

### What did you expect to happen?

When a POD P goes down, the remaining (N-N/M) connections between clients and the other pods are kept intact.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Service with Type Load Balancer and set External Traffic Policy: Local.
2. Establish multiple long running TCP connections from an external client to the service.
3. Horizontally scale the PODs behind the service. For example from 3 to 8.
4. You can see multiple TCP connections are broken from the client side.

title: kube-scheduler preemption logic deadlock when it evicts a Pod with a volume to make room for the CSI driver Pod
body:
### What happened?

We managed to reproduce and verify the following deadlock that occurs when kube-scheduler evicts a Pod (with less priority) to make room for a CSI driver Pod.
1. New csi-driver-node-disk Pod has to be created for Node `worker-1` (caused by autoscaling event like scale-up or Pod lifecycle event). Pod csi-driver-node-disk has PriorityClass `system-node-critical` (`2000001000` priority class value).
2. Node `worker-1` is full and kube-scheduler has to activate the preemption logic (ref https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/) to make room for Pod csi-driver-node-disk. At this time Pod csi-driver-node-disk is in Pending state.
3. kube-scheduler evicts a Pod with **a volume**. But the corresponding Pod deletion hangs forever in Terminating as there is no running `csi-driver-node-disk` Pod for the given Node to perform the unmount operations.

There is no automatic recovery from this case -> csi-driver-node-disk Pod stays forever in Pending, the evicted Pod stays forever in Terminating.

See below for more detailed steps to reproduce.

### What did you expect to happen?

No such deadlock to be possible to be caused in the system

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Prepare a Node that is almost full (cpu or memory). Make sure that all of the running workload on this Pod has volumes

```
$ k describe no worker-1

Allocated resources:
  (Total limits may be over 100 percent, i.e., overcommitted.)
  Resource           Requests          Limits
  --------           --------          ------
  cpu                1887m (98%)       100m (5%)
  memory             1169187818 (39%)  14972Mi (532%)
```

2. Increase the `csi-driver-node-disk` DaemonSet cpu requests high enough to make sure that it won't fit on the Node (simulate a scale-up event by autoscaler)

3. Make sure that the new csi-driver-node-disk Pod fails to be scheduled with:
```
$ k -n kube-system describe po csi-driver-node-disk-4m7vz

Events:
  Type     Reason            Age                  From               Message
  ----     ------            ----                 ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  10m                  default-scheduler  0/2 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
  Warning  FailedScheduling  8m56s (x1 over 10m)  default-scheduler  0/2 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
```

The csi-driver-node-disk Pod has PriorityClass `system-node-critical`.

4. Make sure that kube-scheduler tries to evict 1 of the Pods with lower priority

```
$ k get po
NAME    READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
web-0   1/1     Running       0          21m
web-1   1/1     Running       0          21m
web-2   0/1     Terminating   0          21m
```

5. Make sure the deletion of this web-2 Pod (that has a volume) hangs forever because there is no running csi-driver-node-disk Pod for this Node to perform the unmount operations.

kubelet log:
```
E0617 11:33:53.547111    3074 nestedpendingoperations.go:335] Operation for "{volumeName:kubernetes.io/csi/disk.csi.azure.com^/subscriptions/<omitted>/resourceGroups/shoot--foo--bar/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/pv-shoot--foo--bar-c2561535-78a0-432e-9364-681c36b4d674 podName:ba6a8d0c-6018-436a-a7cb-83cb61341537 nodeName:}" failed. No retries permitted until 2022-06-17 11:35:55.547035965 +0000 UTC m=+13631.726363595 (durationBeforeRetry 2m2s). Error: "UnmountVolume.TearDown failed for volume \"www\" (UniqueName: \"kubernetes.io/csi/disk.csi.azure.com^/subscriptions/<omitted>/resourceGroups/shoot--foo--bar/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/pv-shoot--foo--bar-c2561535-78a0-432e-9364-681c36b4d674\") pod \"ba6a8d0c-6018-436a-a7cb-83cb61341537\" (UID: \"ba6a8d0c-6018-436a-a7cb-83cb61341537\") : kubernetes.io/csi: mounter.SetUpAt failed to get CSI client: driver name disk.csi.azure.com not found in the list of registered CSI drivers"
```

We also encountered this problem in the production environment. Could you give some suggestions for fixing it? cc @msau42 @sanposhiho @Huang-Wei

To mitigate this issue, scheduler may offer dynamic (or even configurable) preemption preferences when it chose preemption victims. But the problem is unresolvable if feasible victim candidate pod(s) on that node are **all volume-attached**.

> We also encountered this problem in the production environment.

Is there an alternative preemption strategy to preempt other pods to make room for the csi daemon pod?

No, the candidate pods in our cluster are all volume-attached. Can we reserve node resources for some key components in the cluster, such as CSI, CNI, etc. so that when these components are upgraded, the resources will not be occupied by other business pods to avoid preemption

Or can we sense whether key components on the node such as csi, cni, etc. are ready during scheduling? If not, prevent pods that rely on key components from being scheduled to the node. The problem with this solution is that we need to consider the time delay between status reporting and scheduling

>  Can we reserve node resources for some key components in the cluster, such as CSI, CNI, etc 

If you mean something like **kube-reserved**, yes, we do, but they're not for pods. https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/reserve-compute-resources/#kube-reserved

> > Can we reserve node resources for some key components in the cluster, such as CSI, CNI, etc
> 
> If you mean something like **kube-reserved**, yes, we do, but they're not for pods. https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/reserve-compute-resources/#kube-reserved

Yes, we use kube-reserved to reserve resources for key processes on the node such as kubelet. Here we hope to reserve resources for key pods in the cluster. We can do this resource reservation at the scheduler level.

Isn't this a problem in the node or CSI side? If the Pod is stuck in termination, there is nothing scheduler can do.

@kubernetes/sig-storage-misc, any ideas?

> Isn't this a problem in the node or CSI side? If the Pod is stuck in termination, there is nothing scheduler can do.
> 
> @kubernetes/sig-storage-misc, any ideas?

Could we reserve resources for key pods in the cluster to prevent this deadlock.
You could use a taint that your CSI driver can remove when it's ready

> You could use a taint that your CSI driver can remove when it's ready
In some scenarios, we will upgrade the resource request of the CSI driver. If the resources on the node are not enough, preemption will occur. Because our business pods all use PVC, this kind of deadlock will also occur. In this scenario, can kubelet be optimized to solve this problem when the pod is deleted and storage resources are released? cc @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs

Resource reservation can help with this but we're far from that, and that's beyond the scope of scheduler, also involves other components like kubelet etc.. 

But a simplified implementation is a resource reservation only work for scheduler and plumbed into scheduler framework as a plugin.

title: Kubelet does not respect container-log-max-size on time, during heavy log writes from container
body:
### What happened?

We are running a Statefulset that logs pretty aggressively on disk. The rate is around 6M/second. The kubelet configs around container log management are set to:
- container-log-max-files: 5
- container-log-max-size: 50Mi

We are running with containerd as the CRI on Kubernetes version 1.20. 


For this specific workload, we notice that the logs DO NOT get rotated upon hitting the 50Mi limit. Instead, the rotation happens at a much later size, depending on the number of containers/Pods on the node. In some extreme cases, if there are several Pods that are aggressively logging to disk, on the same node, then the kubelet lets the log size grow up to several tens of GBs before noticing that the log size has grown out of control. Then, it steps in to rotate the logs (compress and replace). 

This problem is letting nodes consume Terabytes of disk space, as opposed to a few hundred MBs of data for logging. 

### What did you expect to happen?

container logs should be rotated out as specified in the container-log-max-size kubelet configuration.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

My coworker (Venkata Gunapati) has a simple repro for the issue using the following Statefulset spec.

Upon applying this spec, we observe that the Pod/container's log file grow beyond 50Mi to uptown 256Mi, before rotating the logs. It is obvious how the problem gets extreme when dozens of such Pods run on the same node.


```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: logging-test
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: logging-test
  serviceName: "logging-test"
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: logging-test
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 10
      containers:
      - name: logging-test
        command: ["sh", "-c", "i=1; while [ $i -le 100  ]; do j=1; while [ $j -le 2000 ]; do echo 2022-06-16T20:02:18,308+0000  ; j=$(( j+1 )); done; sleep 0.001; i=$(( i+1 )); done"]
        image: busybox
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The code to `rotateLogs` handles one container at a time, for all containers on the node. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/64e83a7e43afd038b3d5a0179e85099a0958de4c/pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go#L222-L223

This is a serial processing of all the container logs that need rotation, which is a bottleneck in this use case. 

### Kubernetes version

```
$ k version

```

nodes.title: kubelet: enable configurable rotation duration and parallel rotate
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Current implementation of the `container_log_manager.go` works with the following behavior 

1. It monitors the logs every 10seconds (not configurable)
2. Rotates the logs in a single loop one after the other for each container. 

This behavior causes a few issues with increase in rate at which the containers will start logging. As suggested in #110630 for example where the containers were generating logs at a monumentally high rate of 6M/second. 

Due to the time required to iterate over each container, compress and rotate the files, the log rotation can never really honor the configured value of `container-log-max-files` and `container-log-max-size` on a cluster with this high log generation rate + a large number of such pods running on the cluster. 

##### What this PR does to mitigate this is enable two things. 

1. Enable Parallel log rotation based on a work queue
2. Enable configurable Duration for monitoring the logs for rotation. This can enable a faster more suitable monitoring duration for the logs based on your cluster's log generation capability requirements.

##### How does this PR enable it ?

It adds two additional configuration to the kubelet's configuration parameters

1. `containerLogMaxWorkers`
2. `containerLogMonitorInterval`

One that cater to enable parallel log rotation with a configurable number of workers based on the pod running capacity and the log generation capacity of the cluster and the other to configure how Frequently the logs are monitored and rotated. 

##### How does this work ?

When the container log manager is started off, it creates n equal to `ContainerLogMaxWorkers` number of go routine based workers that are responsible for ensuring the log rotation workflow for the pods in the cluster. A loop running at an interval defined by `ContainerLogMonitorPeriod` lists all the containers and finds out the running containers and pushes that into a Queue. 

This queue is then processed by the worker to rotate the logs.

Currently, there is a wait loop in the tail end to ensure the queue is empty before handing over the control back for the next iteration of the monitoring based on `ContainerLogMonitorPeriod` to avoid the same container getting processed by multiple workers at the same time. 

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #110630

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Enabled a mechanism for concurrent log rotatation via `kubelet` using a configuration entity of `containerLogMaxWorkers` which controls the maximum number of concurrent rotation that can be performed and an interval configuration of `containerLogMonitorInterval` that can aid is configuring the monitoring duration to best suite your cluster's log generation standards.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:
```docs
NA
```


#### Additional Note
I am hoping to get some suggestion on the following

1. I intend to feature gate this so that we can fallback to the old behavior in case if things don't work out as intended. Is there a guidelines for this ? Should there be a KEP first ?
2. This also introduces two new Attributes to the kubelet's configuration parameters. i.e API change. Should this go via the KEP first ?

#### Note to Reviewers
Even with this fix, the log rotation will not be perfect. Considering the fact that we run the log rotation from outside and via a regular interval based lookup, this will work more or less like how the logrotate like infra would do the job. i.e The size of the file can always exceed the max capped size of the log before we actually rotate it via the kubelet. 

The safest way to ensure the rotation of the log as close to the limit as defined in teh config is to setup a notify watch for each log file in question and rotate them. But that can prove to be a really costly operation to be dealt with when the number of containers are really large in size. Also terminating the notify when the pod is deleted or terminated can be an additonal overhead to deal with. But I am happy explore further into that as well if someone thinks that is the better way to rotate and manage the logs.

Hi, we got the same issue, could someone confirm whether this issue has been fixed? we're using 1.20.7.

/reopen

I am able to reproduce it with v1.29, but only with dirty hacks. Something bad must happen during node reboot.

1. Run a Pod that uses a CSI volume + **file** on the volume as a subpath.
2. Stop kubelet service on the node where the pod runs.
3. Force-delete the Pod.
4. Manually remove vol_data.json from the pod local volume directory, i.e. `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod_UID>/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/<pv_name>/vol_data.json`. I don't know how to reproduce the issue without this step. How else can it happen that the file gets missing or its reconstruction fails?!
5. Hard reboot the machine.

After reboot, newly started kubelet will not see the Pod in the API server, and it will try to reconstruct its CSI volume mount from vol_data.json. That file is missing, and therefore it will declare the volume as unmounted and cleaned, without cleaning its subpaths.

The orphan cleanup routine will then try to remove subpaths of the volume, but it can handle only directories as subpath, not files -> `rmdir` will fail.

nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Allow kubelet orphan cleanup to delete both files and empty directories used as subpath mount points.

A pod does not need to use a directory as a subpath, it can use a file (unix domain socket, pipe, ...) too. Therefore the cleanup should use `os.Remove` that deletes both files and empty directories.

This contrasts with whole volumes - a volume is always a directory.
